text:
And now she began to speak, eager to win him back. She said that it had not been her intention to abandon him forever, but that for a time they had to break off their relationship for appearance’s sake. He had surely seen for himself that her father stood on the threshold of madness, that her mother was in constant danger of her life. He must surely understand that she had been compelled to go home.

Then his anger burst forth in words. She need not pretend. He no longer wished to be her plaything. She had abandoned him as soon as she had been able to go home, and he could no longer love her. When he had come home from the hunt the day before yesterday and found her gone without a greeting, without a word, his blood had frozen in his veins; he had come close to dying of grief. He could not love the woman who had caused him such great pain. Besides, she had never loved him. She was a coquette who wanted someone to kiss and caress her here in her home district as well; that was all.

Did he think, then, that she was in the habit of letting young gentlemen caress her?

Oh yes, he certainly did think so. Women were not as holy as they looked. Selfishness and coquetry from beginning to end! No, if only she had known how he had felt when he came home from the hunt! It was as though he had been wading through ice water. He would never overcome that pain. It would follow him throughout his life. He could never be a human being again.

She tried to explain to him how everything had happened. She sought to remind him that she was still faithful.

Yes, it was all the same, for now he no longer loved her. Now he had seen through her. She was selfish. She did not love him. She had left without giving him a greeting.

He returned to this incessantly. She almost enjoyed the scene. She could not become angry. She understood his anger so well. Nor did she fear any real breach. Yet at last she grew uneasy. Had such a change really taken place in him that he could no longer care for her?

“Gösta!” she said. “Was I selfish when I went to Sjö to fetch the Major? I did remember that they had smallpox there. Nor is it pleasant to walk outdoors in thin shoes in cold and snow.”

“Love lives on love, not on services and good deeds,” said Gösta.

“Then you want us to be strangers from now on, Gösta?”

“I do.”

“Gösta Berling is very changeable.”

“I am commonly accused of such things.”

He was cold, impossible to warm, and in truth she herself was colder still. Self-observation sat there, sneering at her attempts to play the woman in love.

“Gösta!” she said, making one more effort. “I have never intentionally wronged you, though it may look that way. I beg you: forgive me!”

“I cannot forgive you.”

She knew that if she had possessed one wholehearted feeling, she would have won him back. And she tried to act passionate. The eyes of ice mocked her, but she tried all the same. She did not want to lose him.

“Do not go, Gösta! Do not go in anger! Think how ugly I have become! No one can love me anymore.”

“Nor do I,” he said. “You must resign yourself to seeing your heart trampled underfoot, as others do.”

“Gösta, I have never been able to love anyone but you. Forgive me! Do not abandon me! You are the only one who can save me from myself.”

He pushed her away.

“You are not telling the truth,” he said with icy calm. “I do not know what you want with me, but I can see that you are lying. Why do you want to hold on to me? You are so rich that you will never lack suitors.”

With that, he left.

And no sooner had he closed the door than longing and pain, in all their majesty, made their entrance into Marianne’s heart.

It was love, the child of her own heart, emerging from the corner to which the eyes of ice had banished him. He came, the long-awaited one, now, when it was too late. Now he stepped forth, solemn and almighty, and longing and pain bore up his royal mantle.

When Marianne could say to herself with true certainty that Gösta Berling had abandoned her, she experienced a purely physical pain, so terrible that she was almost numbed. She pressed her hands against her heart and sat for hours in the same place, struggling with tearless grief.

And it was she herself who suffered, not a stranger, not an actress. It was she herself.

Why had her father come and separated them? Her love had surely not been dead. It was only in her weakened state after the illness that she had been unable to feel its power.

O God, O God, that she had lost him! O God, that she had awakened so late!

Ah, he was the only one, he was the ruler of her heart! From him she could endure anything. Harshness and cruel words from him merely bowed her down into humble love. If he had struck her, she would have crawled to him like a dog and kissed his hand.

She snatched up pen and paper and wrote with terrible eagerness. First she wrote of her love and longing. Then she begged, not for his love, only for his mercy. It was some kind of verse that she wrote.

She did not know what to do to gain relief from this dull pain.

When she had finished, she thought that if he were to see this, he would surely believe that she loved him. Well, why should she not send what she had written to him? The next day she would send it off, and she felt sure that it would bring him back to her.

The next day she went about in anguish and at war with herself. What she had written seemed so pitiful and foolish to her. It had neither rhyme nor meter. It was only prose. Surely he would only laugh at such verses.

Her pride awakened as well. If he no longer loved her, then it was such a terrible humiliation to beg for his love.

At times prudence came and told her that she ought to be glad that she had escaped from the relationship with Gösta and all the miserable circumstances it would bring with it.

Yet the torments of her heart were so terrible that in the end her feelings were allowed to prevail. Three days after the day on which she had become conscious of her love, she had had the verses placed in an envelope and Gösta Berling’s name written on the wrapper. But they were not sent. Before she had found a suitable messenger, she had heard such things about Gösta Berling that she realized it was already too late to win him back.
